title: Stepped Concurrency Experiment Log - Vasu
content:
Purpose:
Quick, personal log of stepped-concurrency runs to understand p95/p99 behaviour as we scale concurrent request slots on a single GPU pod (A100-80GB). Want to reproduce the weird non-linear tail increase seen in Canary yesterday and try a few mitigation knobs (batch_timeout, max_batch_tokens, KV cache warm fraction).

Environment:
- Model: rw-llama2-13B-fp16 (baseline), quantized variant q4f16 in separate run
- Hardware: A100-80GB, 8 CPU cores assigned to runtime, 64GB host RAM
- Runtime flags: --enable-continuous-batching, --max-batch-tokens=2048 (varied), --batch-timeout-ms varied
- Client: synthetic Poisson generator (locally patched), sustained target qps adjusted to match concurrency
- Warm cache profiles: cold (empty KV), partial-warm (50% prefix hits), warm (>90% prefix hits)
- Measurement window: 5 minute steady-state after warmup for each step
- Observability hooks: p50/p95/p99, cpu/gpu utilization, batch size distribution, queue depth, batch timeout triggers

Experiment plan (stepped concurrency):
- Steps: [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32] concurrent inflight requests
- For each step: ramp 60s -> steady 300s -> cool down 60s
- Repeat for three batch-timeout values: 5ms, 20ms, 50ms
- Run with cold and warm KV cache variants for 2 permutations (cold/warm)

Raw results (median of run window, approximate):
| Step | Concurrency | Target QPS | median(ms) | p95(ms) | p99(ms) | mean batch size | batch timeout triggers/s | GPU util% | Notes |
|------|-------------|-----------:|-----------:|--------:|--------:|----------------:|------------------------:|---------:|------|
| A1   | 1           | 10         | 55         | 68      | 82      | 1.0             | 0.2                     | 12       | baseline
| A2   | 2           | 18         | 58         | 75      | 95      | 1.1             | 0.6                     | 18       | slight tail growth
| A3   | 4           | 32         | 62         | 78      | 130     | 1.7             | 1.8                     | 28       | occasional batching, p99 jumps
| A4   | 8           | 56         | 70         | 120     | 320     | 3.9             | 8.5                     | 58       | big p99 increase, queueing observed
| A5   | 16          | 95         | 85         | 260     | 820     | 6.2             | 21.0                    | 86       | severe tailing, some timeouts
| A6   | 32          | 180        | 160        | 610     | 1400    | 8.1             | 48.2                    | 96       | saturation, long queues

Notes on the above:
- Non-linear tail: p99 jumps dramatically between concurrency 4->8 and again at 8->16. Not simply proportional to QPS.
- Batch formation: mean batch size increases with concurrency (expected) but batch-timeout triggers also increase, suggesting queue growth and time spent waiting for batch completion.
- GPU util climbs toward saturation at high concurrency; however p99 increases even before GPU fully saturated (seen at concurrency 8 where GPU util ~58%). Suggests queueing inside runtime or lock contention.
- Cold vs warm KV cache: warm runs reduce median by ~8-12ms and p95 by ~20-30ms at low concurrency; at high concurrency (>=16) warm cache benefit diminishes — likely because compute bottleneck dominates and KV access is not the limiting factor.
- Batch timeout variation: 5ms -> lower p99 at low concurrency but increases droplet of small batches under load (inefficient GPU packing). 50ms -> larger batches, better amortization but increases queuing latency in tail when request arrival bursts occur. 20ms looked like sweet spot for our model in these runs.

Additional micro-observations (onmetrics):
- Host CPU sys% spikes coincide with p99 outliers; suspect background GC/serialization stalls in runtime.
- Observed a handful of RPC retransmits from client due to transient 5xx at concurrency 16 (reproducible with small probability) — need to correlate with runtime logs (INF-4823).
- Batch size distribution: long tail (many small batches + some huge ones) -> variance in per-token compute time across batch sizes may amplify tail.

Quick actions / next runs to try (TODOs):
- [ ] Run step-up but with randomized jitter on arrival to avoid synchronised bursts (Poisson vs deterministic stepping). Hypothesis: micro-synchronization causes big p99 jumps.
- [ ] Instrument runtime lock contention counters and queueing latencies more precisely (add histograms for wait time before entering batch execution).
- [ ] Try adaptive batch max (cap on max batch tokens per concurrency) to prevent single huge batch causing long execution and blocking others.
- [ ] Re-run with different model variants (q4f16) to see if quantization changes compute vs memory tradeoff and tail behaviour.
- [ ] Correlate p99 outliers with host-level logs (docker pause, oom-kill? unlikely but check).

Notes to self:
- Keep the 20ms batch-timeout as baseline for further experiments on this node type.
- For customer-facing guidance, call out that "predictable p99" requires tuning batch_timeout + concurrency caps; single-number autoscale isn't enough.

Loose hypothesis: tail is caused by a combination of queueing behind long-executing large batches and occasional host-level stalls (serialization/GC). Mitigation should be multi-pronged: limit max batch tokens, small batch-timeout, and break up very large requests (if possible).

References / links: INF-4823 for the Canary failure, PR #1294 for batch-timeout telemetry patch. Slack thread #eng-serving-runtime: thread where Kendra pasted heatmaps (search 'p99 heatmap 2024-10-06').

Appendix: Raw command used for single run (example):
./run_bench --model rw-llama2-13B-fp16 --concurrency 8 --target-qps 56 --batch-timeout-ms 20 --duration 360 --kv-warm 0 --notes "A4" --trace true

End log.
